signal.title: BIST 100
signal.standing: The 100 largest and most traded companies on Borsa İstanbul, Türkiye's only stock exchange. It is priced in lira, so the level carries the country's inflation as much as its earnings: read the direction, not the number.

signal.title: Ibovespa
signal.standing: The most traded shares on B3, the São Paulo exchange that is Latin America's largest, weighted by market value. Iron ore, oil and Brazilian interest rates drive it, through the miners, oil producers and banks that dominate it.

signal.title: IDX Composite
signal.standing: Every company listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in Jakarta, counted in one index. It is the market of the world's largest Muslim-majority country, and commodity producers and banks carry most of its weight.

signal.title: IPC
signal.standing: The Índice de Precios y Cotizaciones tracks about 35 of the largest, most traded companies on the Bolsa Mexicana de Valores in Mexico City. It is Mexico's benchmark, tightly coupled to US demand and the peso.

signal.title: TA-125
signal.standing: The 125 largest companies by market value on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, Israel's only stock market. It trades Sunday to Thursday and is heavily weighted to banks, defence and technology.

signal.title: SMI
signal.standing: The Swiss Market Index: the 20 largest companies on the SIX Swiss Exchange in Zurich, Switzerland's main market. Nestlé, Roche and Novartis carry it, which makes it defensive when the world turns risk-off.

signal.title: SET Index
signal.standing: A capitalisation-weighted index of every common stock on the Stock Exchange of Thailand in Bangkok, the country's main market. It is sensitive to tourism flows and regional energy prices.

signal.title: FTSE/JSE All Share
signal.standing: The All Share index covers nearly every company listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, South Africa's main market, weighted by size. It is Africa's largest exchange by far, and the only one with a usable public daily series.

signal.title: S&P/TSX Composite
signal.standing: The broad benchmark of the Toronto Stock Exchange, Canada's main market, tracking around 200 of its largest companies by market value. Banks, oil producers and miners dominate it, so it trades like a commodity index.

signal.title: TAIEX
signal.standing: The Taiwan Stock Exchange's capitalisation-weighted index of every common share listed in Taipei. TSMC alone is roughly a third of it, which makes this the most concentrated major market on the map.

signal.title: Straits Times Index
signal.standing: The 30 largest and most traded companies on the Singapore Exchange, the main market of Southeast Asia's financial hub. Three banks and regional property groups carry most of its weight, so it moves with interest rates.

signal.title: SENSEX
signal.standing: The Sensitive Index: 30 of the largest companies on the Bombay Stock Exchange in Mumbai, India. The exchange is Asia's oldest, founded in 1875, and this index is the benchmark for Indian equities.

signal.title: S&P 500
signal.standing: An index of 500 large companies listed on US stock exchanges, weighted by market value. It is the benchmark most pension and index funds are measured against, and a handful of technology firms carry much of its weight.

signal.title: Nasdaq-100
signal.standing: The 100 largest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq exchange in New York, weighted by size. A handful of technology giants make up most of it, so it reads as the price of American big tech.

signal.title: KOSPI
signal.standing: The Korea Composite Stock Price Index: every company on the main board of the Korea Exchange in Seoul, weighted by size. Samsung and SK Hynix dominate it, so it moves with the global semiconductor cycle.

signal.title: Nikkei 225
signal.standing: The Nikkei 225 tracks 225 large companies on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, Japan's main market, weighted by share price. Tokyo is Asia's largest exchange and the first major market to price each trading day.

signal.title: Hang Seng
signal.standing: The Hang Seng Index tracks the largest and most traded companies on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. It is where mainland Chinese companies meet foreign capital, and the clearest daily read on sentiment toward China.

signal.title: DFM General
signal.standing: The main index of the Dubai Financial Market, the stock exchange in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. It is the Gulf's main listing venue for property and banking, and trades Monday to Friday, unlike Riyadh.

signal.title: FTSE 100
signal.standing: The 100 largest companies listed on the London Stock Exchange, Britain's main market, ranked by market value. Most of their revenue is earned abroad, so a falling pound tends to push the index up.

signal.title: DAX
signal.standing: The Deutscher Aktienindex: the 40 largest companies on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, Germany's main market. It is built on the country's industrial and chemical base, making it Europe's clearest export barometer.

signal.title: CAC 40
signal.standing: The 40 largest companies listed on Euronext Paris, France's main stock market, weighted by the value of their freely traded shares. Luxury and energy groups dominate it, leaving it unusually exposed to Chinese consumer demand.

signal.title: IBEX 35
signal.standing: The 35 most liquid companies on the Bolsa de Madrid, Spain's main stock exchange. Its big banks earn much of their profit in Latin America, so the index moves with both regions.

signal.title: FTSE MIB
signal.standing: The 40 largest, most traded companies on Borsa Italiana in Milan, Italy's main market. Banks and utilities dominate it, making it the market most sensitive to Italian sovereign debt spreads.

signal.title: S&P/ASX 200
signal.standing: The 200 largest companies listed on the Australian Securities Exchange in Sydney, weighted by market value. Mining and banking dominate it, and it is often the first major market to react to Chinese demand data.

validated.text: Turkish stocks on Borsa İstanbul fell 6.7% across 4 straight sessions from 2026-10-13 to 2026-10-19. The slide came during a week of domestic news, including a police raid on opposition broadcaster Halk TV and record rain flooding Istanbul. No article here links either event to the market's fall.

Indonesian stocks on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in Jakarta lost 20.0% over 20 sessions to 2026-11-04. The slide included a 10% plunge to a six-year low and an 11.6% fall on a Friday, the worst day since 1998. Both days were reported in coverage of MSCI and Indonesia's market status.

Mexican stocks on the Bolsa Mexicana de Valores rose 7.1% over 20 sessions to October 27. In the same weeks, inflation hit 3.62% in early October, above forecasts, and AT&T moved to sell 24.7 million Mexican subscribers for $2 billion. None of the coverage ties either event to the rise.

Stocks on the Taiwan Stock Exchange fell 16.4% over 20 sessions to 2026-11-09. In the same weeks, Micron workers staged Taiwan's first chip-industry strike, and Taiwan tracked 53 Chinese ships, 34 of them warships. None of the coverage links either event to the fall in Taipei.

Indian stocks on the Bombay Stock Exchange rose 10.7% over 8 straight sessions. The run began the day Jio Platforms shares rose 21.4% after India's largest initial public offering, and the day likely central-bank dollar sales lifted the rupee to 95.02. No supplied report links the rally to either.

Stocks on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange rose 8.0% over 5 straight sessions to 2026-11-05. The run came alongside news that Nvidia and Pika now build on MiniMax's Chinese video model, and that China's trade surplus hit a record $938.1 billion through September. The coverage does not link either to the gain.

Israeli stocks on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange fell 7.3% over 5 straight sessions to 2026-11-05. The slide coincided with the opening of coalition talks, in which 19 Arab-party seats decide who governs Israel, and with Trump saying $4 billion in Israel aid stops at year-end. None of the reports links either to the market.

Japanese stocks on the Tokyo Stock Exchange fell 11.2% over 5 straight sessions, from October 29 to November 6. The slide came as a sell-off spread across Asia: on Friday South Korea halted trading after the Kospi fell 8%. In the same week the yen rose 0.7% against the dollar.
